name: Middle Palaeolithic burial and ochre ritual
summary: The earliest intentional burials with red ochre and grave goods (Skhul, Qafzeh, Tinshemet) and engraved ochre in southern Africa (Blombos). Made by early Homo sapiens and Neanderthals; meaning is inferred, not known.

name: Aboriginal Australian religion (the Dreaming)
summary: The Dreaming (Tjukurpa, Jukurrpa, Altyerre): law carried in country, song and ceremony. Start reflects human arrival in Australia (c. 65,000–50,000 years ago); how far back present-day traditions reach is a matter of Indigenous tradition and scholarly debate.

name: Papuan religions of New Guinea
summary: Hundreds of local traditions; start reflects human settlement of New Guinea.

name: Andamanese religion
summary: Religion of the peoples of the Andaman Islands (Great Andamanese, Önge, Jarawa), recorded by A. R. Radcliffe-Brown in 1906–08: a great being of the north-east monsoon, spirits of the sea and forest, and the spirits of the dead. In the peace-making dance of the North Andaman two parties of former enemies act out their anger and then weep together, and boys and girls pass through ceremonies at puberty. The dates are those of the islands’ first settlement, disputed (24,000 to 50,000 years ago).

name: Upper Palaeolithic art and ritual
summary: Figurines (the lion-man, 'Venus' figures), painted caves (Chauvet, Lascaux), music and rich burials (Sungir) across Ice Age Eurasia. Often read as evidence of shamanism and animal spirits.

name: San religion
summary: Trance dance and /Kaggen; rock art from c. 30,000 years ago (Apollo 11 Cave) is attributed to San ancestors.

name: Jōmon ritual
summary: Clay dogū figurines, stone circles and burial practices of Japan's long-lived foraging culture.

name: Natufian ritual and burial
summary: First settled foragers of the Levant: cemeteries, skull removal, funeral feasts and the earliest known shaman burial (Hilazon Tachtit, c. 12,000 years ago).

name: Neolithic cults of Anatolia and the Levant
summary: Monumental enclosures with carved T-pillars (Göbekli Tepe, Karahan Tepe, Nevalı Çori), plastered ancestor skulls (Jericho), lime-plaster statues ('Ain Ghazal) and the house shrines of Çatalhöyük.

name: Neolithic figurine cults of Old Europe
summary: Thousands of clay figurines, house shrines and signs (Vinča, Cucuteni–Trypillia, the Tărtăria tablets) in the Balkans and Danube basin.

name: Saharan Neolithic cattle cult
summary: Cattle burials, stone alignments and a stone circle at Nabta Playa, among herders of the then-green Sahara; sometimes linked to later Egyptian cattle goddesses.

name: Megalithic religion of Atlantic Europe
summary: Passage tombs, stone rows and circles from Brittany to Ireland, Britain and Scandinavia (Carnac, Newgrange, Stonehenge, Orkney), many aligned on the sun at the solstices.

name: Neolithic ritual cultures of China
summary: Jade ritual objects, altars and the 'Goddess Temple' of the Hongshan culture (Niuheliang) and the jade cong and bi of Liangzhu; possible roots of later Chinese ritual.

name: Proto-Indo-European religion (reconstructed)
summary: Reconstructed from shared words and myths of Indo-European peoples: a sky father (*Dyēus), a dawn goddess (*H₂éwsōs), a thunder god and horse sacrifice. Homeland and dates are debated.

name: Sumerian religion
summary: City gods (An, Enlil, Enki, Inanna) served in temples; roots in the Ubaid-period shrine at Eridu (from c. 5400 BCE); absorbed into Babylonian religion.

name: Maltese Temple Culture
summary: Builders of free-standing megalithic temples on Malta and Gozo.

name: Ancient Egyptian religion
summary: Pharaonic religion of Ra, Osiris, Isis, Horus, Ptah and Amun; temple cult closed by Christian emperors (Philae last, c. 537).

name: Archaic mound-builder religion
summary: Earliest ceremonial mound complexes of North America (Watson Brake, Poverty Point).

name: Harappan (Indus Valley) religion
summary: Religion of the Indus civilisation (Great Bath, seals, figurines); script undeciphered and links to later Indian religion debated.

name: Andean religion
summary: Pachamama, the apus (mountain lords) and huacas; living in Quechua and Aymara practice.

name: Norte Chico (Caral) religion
summary: Platform mounds and sunken plazas of the oldest civilisation of the Americas.

name: Elamite religion
summary: Gods Inshushinak, Humban and Kiririsha; absorbed under the Achaemenids.

name: Orang Asli religions
summary: Animist religions of Peninsular Malaysia's first peoples.

name: Canaanite religion
summary: El, Baal, Asherah, Anat and Mot as known from Ebla and Ugarit; continued in Phoenician, Israelite and Transjordanian religion.

name: Kushite (Nubian) religion
summary: Kerma-culture religion, later Amun of Jebel Barkal and the lion god Apedemak of Meroë.

name: Babylonian and Assyrian religion
summary: Akkadian-speaking continuation of Sumerian religion (Marduk, Ashur, Ishtar, Shamash, Sin); temple cult faded by the 1st–3rd c. CE.

name: Hurrian religion
summary: Teshub, Hebat and Kumarbi; deeply shaped Hittite and Ugaritic religion.

name: Anitism (Philippine Indigenous religion)
summary: Veneration of anito and diwata led by babaylan, from Austronesian settlement onward.

name: Korean shamanism (Muism)
summary: Mudang shamans perform gut rituals for gods and ancestors.

name: Minoan religion
summary: Bronze Age Cretan religion of goddesses, peak sanctuaries and bull-leaping.

name: Luwian religion
summary: Religion of the Luwian-speaking peoples of southern and western Anatolia and northern Syria: the storm god Tarhunt, the moon god Arma and the goddess Kubaba of Carchemish are known from Hittite texts and hieroglyphic inscriptions. The Hittite state religion took many Luwian gods into itself.

name: Harranian religion (Sabians of Harran)
summary: Moon-god Sin cult of Harran, mentioned in the Mari letters; survived as the 'Sabians' under Islamic rule until the 11th c.

name: Nuragic religion
summary: Sardinian Bronze and Iron Age cult of sacred wells and bronze figurines.

name: Hittite religion
summary: 'Thousand gods of Hatti': state cult of the Storm God and the Sun Goddess of Arinna, absorbing Hattic, Hurrian and Luwian gods.

name: Ancient Greek religion
summary: Olympian gods already named on Mycenaean Linear B tablets; public cult banned in the 390s CE.

name: Shang religion
summary: Worship of ancestors and the high god Di through oracle-bone divination and sacrifice.

name: Astrology (Western)
summary: The reading of the heavens for meaning, from the Babylonian omen series (by about 1000 BCE) to the horoscopes of Greek-speaking Egypt and Rome (from about 200 BCE), and on through Islamic, medieval and modern astrology: divination, philosophy and practice, not a church.

name: Kassite religion
summary: Religion of the Kassites, a people of the Zagros hills who ruled Babylon for about four centuries. They kept their own gods (Shuqamuna and Shumaliya, Harbe, the storm god Buriash) and took up Babylon’s; their boundary stones carry the emblems of the gods.

name: Chamorro religion
summary: Puntan and Fu'una creation; ancestor spirits (taotaomo'na).

name: Micronesian religions
summary: Navigation lore, ancestor spirits and sacred chiefs.

name: Olmec religion
summary: Earliest Mesoamerican religion: were-jaguar, maize god and colossal heads.

name: Vedic religion (Brahmanism)
summary: Fire sacrifice (yajna) to Indra, Agni, Soma and Varuna; developed into classical Hinduism.

name: Zoroastrianism
summary: Worship of Ahura Mazda taught by Zarathustra. His dates are contested: linguistic evidence points to c. 1500–1000 BCE, some scholars argue for the 7th–6th c. BCE.

name: Atenism
summary: Akhenaten's exclusive worship of the sun disk Aten; reversed after his death.

name: Chavín religion
summary: Oracle temple of the Lanzón deity.

name: Israelite religion
summary: Worship of YHWH in the kingdoms of Israel and Judah; developed into Judaism after the Babylonian exile.

name: Moabite religion
summary: National cult of Chemosh, known from the Mesha Stele.

name: Phoenician and Punic religion
summary: Baal, Astarte, Melqart, Eshmun, Tanit and Baal Hammon; carried across the Mediterranean with Carthage.

name: Edomite religion
summary: National religion of Edom, the kingdom south-east of the Dead Sea, whose chief god was Qos (Qaus); known from Assyrian records, personal names and the Hebrew Bible. The Edomites went on as the Idumeans of the Hellenistic age.

name: Ammonite religion
summary: National religion of Ammon, the kingdom of Rabbath-Ammon (now Amman), whose god was Milkom, with El; known from the Hebrew Bible, Assyrian records and a few Ammonite inscriptions.

name: Phrygian religion
summary: Religion of the Phrygians of central Anatolia (Gordion, King Midas), who took over an older Anatolian religion in which a Mother goddess held first place: Matar, Cybele to the Greeks. Sabazios and the moon god Men were also Phrygian gods.

name: Philistine religion
summary: Religion of the Philistines, Sea Peoples who settled the coast of Canaan about 1175 BCE: Dagon headed their pantheon, with temples at Ashdod and Gaza. Known from the Hebrew Bible and from Egyptian and Assyrian records; the cult of Dagon outlasted the people.

name: Aramean religion
summary: Hadad of Damascus, Atargatis and Baalshamin; spread across Syria into the Roman era.

name: Kanak religion
summary: Ancestor religion of New Caledonia.

name: Chinese folk religion
summary: Worship of Heaven, ancestors, local gods and immortals, continuous since the Zhou.

name: Amazonian ayahuasca shamanism
summary: Healing with sacred plants and icaros (songs).

name: Ancient Berber (Libyan) religion
summary: Amazigh religion including Ammon of Siwa and Gurzil.

name: Chukchi religion
summary: Arctic shamanism of Chukotka.

name: Chumash religion
summary: Rock art and astronomy.

name: Evenki shamanism
summary: Tungusic shamanism; the word 'shaman' is Evenki.

name: Fijian religion
summary: Degei the serpent god.

name: Finnic religion
summary: Ukko, Väinämöinen and the spirit world of Finns, Karelians and Estonians.

name: Kwaio ancestral religion
summary: Solomon Islands ancestor cult.

name: Maya religion
summary: Itzamna, Kukulkan, the Hero Twins and the 260-day calendar; living Maya spirituality today.

name: Mbuti religion
summary: Forest religion and molimo songs.

name: Pacific Northwest Coast religions
summary: Potlatch, winter ceremonials and crest beings.

name: South Arabian religion
summary: Sabaean and Himyarite worship of Almaqah and Athtar; Himyar turned to monotheism c. 380 CE.

name: Sámi religion
summary: Noaidi shamanism with sacred drums and sieidi stones; suppressed 17th–18th c., now reviving.

name: Sarnaism
summary: Sacred-grove religion of the Munda, Oraon and Ho.

name: Thracian religion
summary: Thracian Horseman, Zalmoxis and Bendis.

name: Vanuatu kastom religion
summary: Custom religion and graded societies.

name: Vedda religion
summary: Ancestor-spirit religion of Sri Lanka's Indigenous people.

name: Yanomami religion
summary: Shamanism of the xapiri spirits.

name: Lycian religion
summary: Religion of the Lycians of south-west Anatolia, a people whose language, Lycian, is related to Luwian, centred on the sanctuary of Leto (the Letoon) near Xanthos; Lycian inscriptions and rock-cut tombs show Anatolian gods beside Greek ones. Herodotus (I.173) is the older Greek source.

name: Illyrian religion
summary: Religion of the Illyrian peoples of the western Balkans, known from Roman-period inscriptions and finds rather than from any text of their own: local gods such as Bindus, equated with Neptune, and the horseman Medaurus, with sun and serpent signs on metalwork and stones.

name: Basque religion before Christianity
summary: The old religion of the Basque-speaking peoples is known only from Strabo, a few Roman-period dedications to local gods and folklore written down from the 1800s (Basa-Jaun the wild man, the lamiak or fairies); how much of the folklore is old is disputed.

name: Shrauta (Vedic) ritual tradition
summary: The solemn Vedic fire sacrifices set out in the Brahmanas and Shrauta Sutras: the Agnihotra (morning and evening milk-offerings into the fire), the offering of first-fruits, the seasonal sacrifices (Chaturmasya), the Soma sacrifices and the building of the fire altar, still kept by small communities of priests in India.

name: Koryak religion
summary: Religion of the Koryak of north-east Siberia and Kamchatka, recorded by Waldemar Jochelson in 1900–01: a Supreme Being, Big-Raven as the first man and ancestor, and spirits of land and sea. The dates are the same placeholder as the map data’s Chukchi record.

name: Yukaghir religion
summary: Religion of the Yukaghir of the Kolyma and Indigirka rivers in north-east Siberia: shamans, and the cult of the clan ancestor, which Jochelson found already fading in the 1890s; the Yukaghir are now very few. The dates are a placeholder like the map data’s Chukchi record.

name: Etruscan religion
summary: The 'Etruscan discipline' of divination, held in the tradition to have been revealed; haruspices were still consulted in Rome in 408 CE.

name: Urartian religion
summary: State cult of the god Haldi at Musasir and Tushpa.

name: Polynesian religion
summary: Tangaroa, Tāne, Rongo and Tū; mana and tapu; from the Lapita settlement of Tonga and Samoa.

name: Tongan religion
summary: Hikule'o and Maui.

name: Pre-Islamic Arabian religion
summary: Allat, al-Uzza, Manat and Hubal with shrines such as the Kaaba; ended with the spread of Islam (Mecca's idols removed 630).

name: Celtic religion
summary: Religion of Iron Age Celtic peoples (Lugus, Taranis, Epona, Brigid) led by druids.

name: Cult of Cybele (Magna Mater)
summary: Phrygian mother goddess; brought to Rome in 204 BCE.

name: Jainism
summary: Path of non-violence and liberation of the soul; Mahavira's dates are debated (6th or 5th c. BCE).

name: Samoan religion
summary: Tagaloa traditions.

name: Ancient Roman religion
summary: State and household cults of Jupiter, Juno, Mars, Vesta and the Lares; banned by Theodosius I in 391–392.

name: Dionysian Mysteries
summary: Ecstatic initiation cult of Dionysus.

name: Eleusinian Mysteries
summary: Initiation rites of Demeter and Persephone; ended under Theodosius I and the Goths.

name: Umbrian and Oscan religion
summary: Italic religion recorded in the Iguvine Tablets.

name: Mixtec religion
summary: Religion recorded in the Mixtec codices.

name: Mysteries of the Great Gods (Samothrace)
summary: Initiations at the sanctuary of the Great Gods.

name: Scythian religion
summary: Iranian steppe religion described by Herodotus (Tabiti, Papaios, Api).

name: Lydian religion
summary: Religion of the Lydian kingdom of Sardis (Gyges to Croesus, about 680–546 BCE), whose native goddess was Kybebe (Cybele) and whose kings sent rich gifts to Delphi. Little else is known of it; Herodotus is the main source.

name: Armenian pre-Christian religion
summary: Aramazd, Anahit and Vahagn; replaced by Christianity in the early 4th c.

name: Chārvāka (Lokāyata)
summary: Indian materialism.

name: Orphism
summary: Greek mystery tradition of purity and rebirth; gold tablets guided the dead.

name: Iberian religion (pre-Roman Spain)
summary: Religion of the Iberian peoples of eastern and southern Spain before Rome, known from hilltop and cave sanctuaries, votive bronzes and stone figures such as the Lady of Elche; the Iberian language is not yet understood, so few god names survive.

name: Celtiberian and Lusitanian religion
summary: Religion of the Celtiberians of the Spanish plateau and the Lusitanians of the west, known from Roman-period inscriptions that name local gods (Lugus, Endovelicus, Ataecina, Bandua, Reve) and from rock sanctuaries. Lusitanian is Indo-European, but whether it is Celtic is disputed.

name: Sarmatian and Alan religion
summary: Religion of the Sarmatians, Iranian horse-nomads who took the steppe north of the Black Sea from the Scythians, and of their kin the Alans: the Roman historian Ammianus (4th century CE) says the Alans planted a bare sword in the ground and worshipped it as the god of war. The Ossetians are the Alans’ descendants.

name: Judaism
summary: Monotheism of the Jewish people centred on the Torah; Second Temple Judaism after the return from Babylon, Rabbinic Judaism after 70 CE.

name: Pythagoreanism
summary: Religious-philosophical brotherhood teaching transmigration of souls and number mysticism.

name: Buddhism
summary: Path to liberation from suffering taught by the Buddha. His dates are debated: traditional chronology puts his death c. 483 BCE, the 'short chronology' c. 400 BCE.

name: Ājīvika
summary: Ascetic fatalist sect; known only from Jain and Buddhist sources and inscriptions.

name: Baltic religion
summary: Prussian, Lithuanian and Latvian religion (Dievas, Perkūnas, Laima); Lithuania baptised 1387, Samogitia 1413.

name: Bathouism (Bodo)
summary: Worship of Bathoubwrai.

name: Confucianism
summary: Ethical-ritual tradition of the Classics, filial piety and ancestor rites; state orthodoxy for two millennia.

name: Germanic religion
summary: Religion of the continental Germanic peoples (Wodan, Donar, Tiw); continued in Anglo-Saxon and Norse religion.

name: Gondi religion (Koya Punem)
summary: Religion of the Gond people.

name: Guanche religion
summary: Religion of the Indigenous Canary Islanders (Achamán, Chaxiraxi), ended after the Castilian conquest.

name: Guaraní religion
summary: Ñande Ru and the search for the Land without Evil.

name: Hinduism
summary: Family of traditions grounded in the Vedas, dharma, karma and devotion to Vishnu, Shiva, the Goddess and many deities; classical synthesis c. 500 BCE–300 CE.

name: Hmong traditional religion
summary: Shamanic and ancestral religion of the Hmong.

name: Gaelic Irish religion
summary: Religion of the Túatha Dé Danann, recorded later by Christian monks.

name: Kaharingan (Dayak)
summary: Dayak religion; recognised as a form of Hinduism in 1980.

name: Kalash religion
summary: Archaic Indo-Aryan polytheism of the Hindu Kush.

name: Khanty and Mansi religion
summary: Ob-Ugric religion with the bear festival.

name: Khoikhoi religion
summary: Tsui-ǁGoab and Heitsi-eibib.

name: Kirat Mundhum (Kiranti religion)
summary: Ancestral oral scripture and rites of the Limbu, Rai, Sunuwar and Yakkha.

name: Mapuche religion
summary: Ngenechen, machi healers and the ngillatun.

name: Marapu (Sumba)
summary: Ancestor religion of Sumba.

name: Mari Traditional Religion
summary: Sacred-grove religion of the Mari; officially recognised.

name: Khmer neak ta religion
summary: Cult of territorial spirits.

name: Nenets religion
summary: Samoyedic reindeer-herders' religion.

name: Niam Khasi
summary: Religion of the Khasi.

name: Santal religion (Sari Dharam)
summary: Worship of Marang Buru.

name: Toda religion
summary: Buffalo-centred religion of the Nilgiris.

name: Torres Strait Islander religion
summary: Malo-Bomai law and the star Tagai.

name: Tukanoan religion (Desana)
summary: Cosmology of the Vaupés.

name: Udmurt Vos
summary: Religion of the Udmurts.

name: Vietnamese folk religion
summary: Ancestor worship and village tutelary gods.

name: Zapotec religion
summary: Cocijo and ancestor cult; Zapotec calendar books confiscated in 1704.

name: Dacian and Getic religion (Zalmoxis)
summary: Religion of the Getae and Dacians of the lower Danube, Thracian-speaking peoples: Herodotus (IV.94–96) says they believed they did not die but went to the god Zalmoxis. The mountain sanctuaries of Sarmizegetusa Regia, of about 100 BCE–100 CE, are its main remains.

name: Gaulish and Gallo-Roman religion
summary: Religion of the Gauls of France, Belgium and northern Italy, known from Caesar’s account of the druids and gods (Gallic War VI), from the Coligny calendar and from Roman-period dedications to Gaulish gods such as Lugus and Epona, whom the Romans matched to their own.

name: Mohism
summary: Doctrine of universal love and Heaven's will.

name: Samaritanism
summary: Israelite religion centred on Mount Gerizim and the Samaritan Pentateuch; the date of the split from Judaism is debated.

name: Daoism
summary: Way of the Dao: philosophical texts from the 4th c. BCE, organised religion from 142 CE.

name: Nabataean religion
summary: Dushara and Allat worshipped at Petra and Hegra.

name: Zurvanism
summary: Zoroastrian current making Zurvan (Time) the father of Ohrmazd and Ahriman; strong under the Sasanians.

name: Mahāsāṅghika
summary: Early school of the 'Great Community'.

name: Sthaviravāda
summary: Elder school after the first schism; parent of Theravada and Sarvastivada.

name: Druidism (ancient)
summary: Learned priestly class of Gaul and Britain; suppressed by Rome from 54 CE, lasted longer in Ireland.

name: Cult of Isis (Graeco-Roman)
summary: Mystery religion of Isis spread from Ptolemaic Egypt across the Roman Empire.

name: Cult of Serapis
summary: Graeco-Egyptian god created under Ptolemy I; the Serapeum of Alexandria was destroyed in 391.

name: Shinto
summary: Way of the kami honoured at shrines; first written down in the Kojiki (712).

name: Tengrism
summary: Turco-Mongol worship of the Eternal Blue Sky and the Earth.

name: Sarvāstivāda
summary: Influential early school of Kashmir and Gandhara.

name: Theravāda Buddhism
summary: 'Teaching of the Elders' of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

name: Bene Israel
summary: Marathi-speaking Jews of the Konkan coast, by tradition shipwrecked in antiquity.

name: Shaivism
summary: Devotion to Shiva as supreme God.

name: Vaishnavism
summary: Devotion to Vishnu and his avatars Krishna and Rama (Heliodorus pillar c. 113 BCE).

name: Essenes and the Qumran community
summary: Ascetic apocalyptic community associated with the Dead Sea Scrolls.

name: Pharisees
summary: Lay scholars of the oral law; their tradition became Rabbinic Judaism.

name: Sadducees
summary: Priestly party of the Second Temple; disappeared with its destruction.

name: Hopewell religion
summary: Ceremonial earthworks and exchange network.

name: Mahāyāna Buddhism
summary: 'Great Vehicle' of the bodhisattva path.

name: Nazca religion
summary: Geoglyph lines and water cult.

name: Teotihuacan religion
summary: Feathered Serpent, Storm God and the pyramids of Sun and Moon.

name: Roman imperial cult
summary: Worship of deified emperors, beginning with Divus Julius in 42 BCE.

name: Sanamahism (Meitei religion)
summary: Meitei religion of Sanamahi and Lainingthou; eclipsed by Hinduism from 1717, revived since the 1930s.

name: Christianity
summary: Faith in Jesus as Messiah and Son of God, spread by his apostles from Jerusalem.

name: Jewish Christianity (Ebionites, Nazarenes)
summary: Torah-observant followers of Jesus.

name: Chinese Buddhism
summary: Buddhism in China from the 1st c. CE.

name: Saint Thomas Christians
summary: Kerala Christians tracing their origin to St Thomas.

name: Rabbinic Judaism
summary: Judaism of the Mishnah and Talmud, mainstream since late antiquity.

name: Digambara
summary: 'Sky-clad' Jains.

name: Roman Mithraism
summary: Initiatory mystery cult of Mithras popular with Roman soldiers; Iranian roots debated.

name: Śvetāmbara
summary: 'White-clad' Jains; canon fixed at Valabhi c. 453–466.

name: Cochin Jews
summary: Jews of Kerala, recorded on copper plates c. 1000 CE.

name: Gnosticism
summary: Movements teaching salvation through gnosis and a flawed creator; influenced Manichaeism and Mandaeism.

name: Hermeticism
summary: Teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus; revived in the Renaissance and in modern esotericism.

name: Mandaeism
summary: Gnostic baptismal religion revering John the Baptist; origins in the Jordan valley or Mesopotamia are debated.

name: Moche religion
summary: Sacrifice ceremony and the Huacas of Sun and Moon.

name: Sethian Gnosticism
summary: Gnostic group revering Seth; many Nag Hammadi texts.

name: Vietnamese Buddhism
summary: Buddhism in Vietnam from the 2nd c.

name: Alchemy (Western)
summary: Art of changing and perfecting matter and the soul, from the Greek-Egyptian recipes and Zosimos of Panopolis (about 300 CE) through Arabic and Latin alchemy to the Renaissance; it joined chemistry, medicine and religion until the 18th century and lives on in Hermetic and esoteric groups as a spiritual practice.

name: Basilideans
summary: Alexandrian Gnostic school.

name: Valentinianism
summary: Largest Christian Gnostic school, founded in Rome by the Egyptian teacher Valentinus.

name: Way of the Celestial Masters (Zhengyi)
summary: First organised Daoist church, led by hereditary Celestial Masters.

name: Marcionism
summary: Church rejecting the Hebrew Bible's God; first known Christian canon.

name: Madhyamaka
summary: Philosophy of emptiness.

name: Montanism (New Prophecy)
summary: Charismatic prophetic movement.

name: Way of Great Peace
summary: Daoist healing movement behind the Yellow Turban rebellion (184).

name: Cham Balamon Hinduism
summary: Hinduism of the Cham people since the kingdom of Champa.

name: Manichaeism
summary: Dualist world religion founded by Mani; spread from Roman North Africa to China; last communities in Fujian c. 16th–17th c.

name: Neoplatonism
summary: Late Platonist religious philosophy of the One; shaped Christian, Islamic and Jewish mysticism.

name: Christian monasticism
summary: Desert ascetic and communal monastic life, spreading from Egypt.

name: Cult of Sol Invictus
summary: State cult of the Unconquered Sun established by Aurelian.

name: Beta Israel (Haymanot)
summary: Ethiopian Jewish community with a Ge'ez Bible; origins debated; most now live in Israel.

name: Yogācāra
summary: Mind-only philosophy.

name: Pictish religion
summary: The religion of the Picts of northern Scotland before Christianity is almost unknown: the lives of Saints Ninian and Columba mention idols, druids at King Brude’s court near Inverness and a spring worshipped as a god, and the carved symbol stones have no text. Whether the Picts were a Celtic people was long disputed.

name: Armenian Apostolic Church
summary: First state church: traditional date 301, many scholars prefer 314.

name: Donatism
summary: North African rigorist church.

name: Arianism
summary: Teaching that the Son is subordinate to the Father; faith of the Goths, Vandals and Lombards.

name: Georgian Orthodox Church
summary: National church of Georgia since King Mirian III.

name: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church
summary: Church of Ethiopia since King Ezana's conversion; 81-book Bible.

name: Shangqing (Highest Clarity)
summary: Visionary meditation Daoism of Maoshan.

name: Priscillianism
summary: Ascetic movement of Spain and Gaul led by the layman Priscillian, bishop of Ávila, who was beheaded at Trier in 385, the first Christian put to death for heresy by the state. Charged with Manichaean and Gnostic ideas, its followers lasted in north-west Spain until the First Council of Braga (561; older books say 563) renewed the condemnation, and after.

name: Korean Buddhism
summary: Buddhism in Korea from 372 (Goguryeo).

name: Judaism in Himyar
summary: Himyarite kings adopted Judaism; ended by the Aksumite conquest c. 525.

name: Lingbao (Numinous Treasure)
summary: Daoist liturgical tradition influenced by Buddhism.

name: Newar Buddhism
summary: Sanskrit Vajrayana of the Kathmandu Valley.

name: Shaktism
summary: Worship of the Goddess (Devi) as supreme power.

name: Pelagianism
founder: Pelagius (a British monk teaching in Rome) and Caelestius
summary: Teaching of the monk Pelagius and his follower Caelestius that people can choose the good by their own will and that Adam’s sin did not ruin all humankind; Augustine opposed it, and it was condemned at Carthage (418) and Ephesus (431). It is known mostly from its opponents’ writings.

name: Pure Land Buddhism
summary: Devotion to Amitabha Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land.

name: Church of the East
summary: East Syriac church of Persia that reached India, Central Asia and China; today the Assyrian and Ancient Churches of the East.

name: Celtic (Irish) Christianity
summary: Monastic Christianity of Ireland and Britain; aligned with Roman practice after Whitby (664).

name: Anglo-Saxon paganism
summary: Woden, Thunor and Frige in early England.

name: Catholicism (Latin Church)

name: Oriental Orthodoxy

name: Ifugao religion

name: Kalinga religion
summary: Cordillera religion.

name: Kogi and Arhuaco religion

name: Yoruba religion
summary: Worship of Olódùmarè and the òrìṣà (Ọbàtálá, Ògún, Ṣàngó, Ọ̀ṣun, Èṣù) centred on Ile-Ife.

name: Moism (Zhuang)
summary: Zhuang religion of the creator Buluotuo.

name: Kāpālika ascetics (skull-bearers)
summary: Shaiva ascetics of early medieval India who carried a skull as a begging bowl and lived on the cremation grounds; known from inscriptions, Sanskrit plays and satires and the writings of their critics. They had faded by about 1300.

name: Bontoc Igorot religion
summary: Religion of the Bontoc Igorot of the Mountain Province of northern Luzon, recorded by Albert Jenks in 1903: spirits of the dead and of nature (anito), a high being, Lumawig, an exorcist and a priesthood, sacred days, and ceremonies for the crops, for the weather, for taking heads and for the ato (the men’s ward). The dates are a wide placeholder.

name: Tinguian (Itneg) religion
summary: Religion of the Tinguian (Itneg) of Abra in north-west Luzon, recorded by Fay-Cooper Cole in 1907–08: a chief god, Kadaklan, many spirits, and women mediums who summon them in ceremonies such as the Dawak and the Sayang. Cole says ceremonial life fills the months after the rice harvest until the rains of May, some ceremonies being open to all and others kept to certain families. The dates are a wide placeholder.

name: Karen religion
summary: Religion of the Karen of southern Burma and Thailand before and beside Buddhism and Christianity: the high god Y’wa, the soul (k’la), which can wander off (Marshall says Karen families tie their wrists to keep it from going while they build a house), spirits, and the story of a lost book given by God; most Karen are now Buddhist or Christian. The dates are a wide placeholder.

name: Shan religion
summary: Religion of the Shan, a Tai people of north-eastern Burma, who are Theravada Buddhists and also keep the older worship of the phi (spirits), as Mrs. Leslie Milne recorded in the 1900s: the soul, she says, stays near the body for three days after death, the Shans bury their dead, and only monks are burnt. The dates are a wide placeholder.

name: Naga religions (traditional)
summary: Traditional religions of the Naga peoples of north-east India and Burma (Angami, Ao, Sema, Lhota, Konyak and others): spirits of earth, sky, village and the dead, and days of restriction (genna). Hutton records the Angami Sekrengi genna, when the young men sing in a great house and hang small birds and animals on poles before the houses, and the feasts of merit that men seeking fame give, pulling a stone; most Nagas are now Baptist Christians. The dates are a wide placeholder.

name: Syriac Orthodox Church
summary: West Syriac miaphysite church.

name: Benedictine Order
summary: Monastic order following the Rule of St Benedict.

name: Japanese Buddhism
summary: Buddhism in Japan from the 6th c.

name: Nubian Christianity (Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia)
summary: Church of the Christian kingdoms of the middle Nile, converted by missionaries from Byzantine and Coptic Egypt about 543–580; Makuria kept its faith under the baqt treaty with the Arabs (about 652), and Christianity faded between the 14th and 15th centuries under Mamluk pressure and the spread of Islam.

name: Tiantai
summary: Lotus Sutra school.

name: Dongba religion (Naxi)
summary: Naxi priestly religion with pictographic scriptures.

name: Huayan
summary: Flower Garland school.

name: Muisca religion
summary: Sun god Sué and the El Dorado offering at Lake Guatavita.

name: Taíno religion
summary: Zemí spirits, the creator Yúcahu and the cohoba ceremony; modern revival.

name: Vajrayāna (Tantric Buddhism)
summary: Esoteric Buddhism of mantra, mandala and initiation.

name: Islam
summary: Submission to the one God; held to have been revealed in the Quran to Muhammad.

name: Shia Islam
summary: Partisans of Ali and the Imams from Muhammad's family.

name: Sunni Islam
summary: Majority Islam following Muhammad's sunna and the first four caliphs.

name: Tibetan Buddhism
summary: Buddhism of Tibet, Mongolia and the Himalaya.

name: Paulicians
summary: Dualist movement of Armenia and Anatolia.

name: Shugendō
summary: Mountain asceticism blending kami and Buddhas.

name: Kharijites
summary: Seceded from Ali after the arbitration at Siffin.

name: Onmyōdō
summary: Yin-yang divination and calendar magic.

name: Ibadi Islam
summary: Moderate early dissenting school; majority in Oman.

name: Maronite Church
founder: Saint Maron (hermit, died about 410); John Maron, first patriarch
summary: Eastern Catholic church of Lebanon and Syria named for the hermit Saint Maron (died about 410); its patriarchate begins with John Maron about 685, and it has been in communion with Rome since the Crusades at the latest (the Maronites hold that they never broke it). It uses the West Syriac liturgy.

name: Ancestral Puebloan religion
summary: Great kivas and solar alignments of Chaco Canyon.

name: Chuvash religion (Vattisen Yaly)
summary: Religion of the Volga Bulgars' descendants.

name: Smarta tradition
summary: Worship of five deities with Advaita Vedanta philosophy.

name: Sufism
summary: Islamic mysticism of love and union with God.

name: Advaita Vedanta
summary: School of non-dual Vedanta holding that the self (atman) is Brahman and that the many things of the world are appearance (maya); set out by Adi Shankara in the 8th century on the base of Gaudapada, and the philosophy of the Smarta tradition and the Shankara monasteries.

name: Khazar Judaism
summary: Conversion of the Khazar elite to Judaism; extent and date debated.

name: Zaydi Shia
summary: Fiver Shia, historically dominant in northern Yemen.

name: Barghawata religion
summary: Berber religion with its own Quran.

name: Khurramites
summary: Iranian movement descended from Mazdakism; led the revolt of Babak Khorramdin (816–837).

name: Karaite Judaism
summary: Scripture-only Judaism rejecting the authority of the Talmud.

name: Ismaili Shia
summary: Followers of the line of Isma'il; Fatimid caliphate 909–1171.

name: Nyingma
summary: 'Old school' of the first translations.

name: Odinani (Igbo religion)
summary: Worship of Chukwu, the earth goddess Ala and ancestors; Nri priest-kingship.

name: Kashmir Shaivism (Trika)
summary: Non-dual tantric Shaivism.

name: Mississippian religion
summary: Southeastern Ceremonial Complex of Cahokia and Moundville.

name: Korean Seon
summary: Korean Zen; largest order today is the Jogye Order.

name: Songhai traditional religion
summary: Holey spirit possession and Sorko and Zima priests.

name: Magyar religion before Christianity
summary: Religion of the Magyars before they became Christians about 1000: a high god (named Isten in the Library’s 1917 account; whether that was his old name is debated) over many lesser gods of nature, with priests called táltos and sacrifices of white horses; it is known only from a few chronicles, old folk belief and the laws that forbade its rites.

name: Dzogchen (Great Perfection)
summary: The “Great Perfection” teaching of the Nyingma school (and of Bön) that the nature of the mind is already awake and has only to be recognised; Tibetan tradition traces it to Garab Dorje in India and to Padmasambhava and Vimalamitra in the 8th century, while historians find clear evidence only from the 9th–10th centuries.

name: Shingon
summary: Esoteric Buddhism.

name: Tendai
summary: Lotus Sutra school on Mount Hiei.

name: Qalandar and Malamati currents (the way of blame)
summary: Two linked Sufi currents of blame and of casting off the world: the Malamatis of 9th-century Nishapur hid their piety to avoid praise, and the Qalandars, wandering and begging dervishes from about 1200, shaved and left worldly rules behind. The Qalandar way lives on at shrines such as that of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar at Sehwan.

name: Toltec religion
summary: Religion of the Toltecs of Tula (Tollan), centred on the feathered-serpent god Quetzalcoatl, as the Aztecs remembered it. The chronicles disagree (older histories give the empire about 856 to 1060, the Anales de Cuauhtitlan put its priest-king Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl at 923 to 947) and the digs at Tula say about 900 to 1150; how much of the Toltec story is history and how much Aztec legend is much debated.

name: Alawites (Nusayris)
summary: Esoteric Shia community, mainly in Syria.

name: Bulgarian Orthodox Church
summary: Founded with Boris I's baptism; Slavonic liturgy of Cyril and Methodius' disciples.

name: Twelver Shia (Imamiyya)
summary: Largest Shia branch, holding that the Twelfth Imam is hidden and will return.

name: Anishinaabe religion
summary: Gichi-Manidoo, the Seven Fires prophecy.

name: Balinese Hinduism (Agama Hindu Dharma)
summary: Hindu-Buddhist religion of Bali shaped by Majapahit; nationally organised 1959.

name: Bon
summary: Tibetan religion claiming pre-Buddhist roots in Zhang Zhung; organised as Yungdrung Bon from the 11th c.

name: Bugis traditional religion (Tolotang, Bissu)
summary: Pre-Islamic Bugis religion of the La Galigo.

name: Edo religion
summary: Religion of the Benin Kingdom (Osanobua, Olokun).

name: Hawaiian religion
summary: Kū, Kāne, Lono, Kanaloa and Pele; kapu system abolished 1819.

name: Marquesan religion
summary: Tiki and tapu.

name: Society Islands religion
summary: Cult of 'Oro at Taputapuātea.

name: Cluniac Reform
summary: Monastic reform from the Abbey of Cluny.

name: Bogomilism

name: Kālacakra tradition
summary: Tantric Buddhist teaching on time, the body and the cosmos, given in the Kālacakra Tantra (composed in northern India in the 10th–11th centuries) and taken to Tibet in the 11th century; the Tibetan sixty-year calendar starts in 1027, and the tantra tells of the hidden kingdom of Shambhala.

name: Kaifeng Jews
summary: Jewish community of Kaifeng (synagogue 1163); organised life ended in the mid-19th c.

name: Mazu worship
summary: Cult of the sea goddess Lin Moniang.

name: Russian Orthodox Church
summary: From the baptism of Rus' (988); autocephalous 1448, patriarchate 1589.

name: Akan religion
summary: Worship of Onyame, the abosom and ancestors; Asante Odwira festival.

name: Bambara (Bamana) religion
summary: Komo, Kore and Ciwara societies of the Mande world.

name: Buryat shamanism
summary: Shamanism of the Buryats.

name: Cherokee religion
summary: Sacred fire and medicine formulas.

name: Dinka religion
summary: Nhialic and the masters of the fishing spear.

name: Vodun (Fon, Ewe and Aja)
summary: Worship of Mawu-Lisa and the vodun spirits; Fá divination; national holiday in Benin since 1997.

name: Fulbe pastoral religion
summary: Pre-Islamic pastoral initiation lore of the Fulani (Koumen, Kaïdara).

name: Guna religion

name: Bori (Hausa spirit religion)
summary: Possession cult of the iskoki spirits.

summary: Sedna, Sila and the angakkuq.

summary: Order of yogis; founders of hatha yoga.

name: Nuer religion
summary: Kwoth and the prophets.

name: Waaqeffannaa (Oromo religion)
summary: Worship of Waaqa within the Gadaa system (UNESCO 2016).

name: Ossetian traditional religion (Uatsdin)
summary: Folk religion of the Alans' descendants; revived and organised since the 1990s.

name: Rwandan and Burundian religion (Imana)
summary: Imana, sacred kingship and the Ubwiru ritual code.

name: Senufo religion (Poro)

summary: uNkulunkulu, amadlozi ancestors and izangoma diviners.

name: Ibibio religion
summary: Religion of the Ibibio of south-east Nigeria: Obumo, the Thunder God, worshipped at sacred groves, and Eka Abassi, “Mother of God”, whom the inner teaching makes head of the pantheon; the Ekpe and Idiong societies; recorded by P. A. Talbot in the 1910s and 1920s. The dates are a rough placeholder.

name: Ekoi (Ejagham) religion
summary: Religion of the Ekoi (Ejagham) of the Cross River in south-east Nigeria and western Cameroon: a sky god and an earth god (both called Obassi), spirits of the bush and the dead, and secret societies. The dates are a rough placeholder.

name: Thonga (Tsonga) religion
summary: Religion of the Thonga (Tsonga) of southern Mozambique and the Transvaal: the spirits of the ancestors, to whom people offer the mhamba, any object by which they enter into relation with them (at a burial, a twig held by the officiant), diviners, rain and fertility beliefs, and the circumcision school (ngoma), as recorded by Henri Junod in 1912–13. The dates are a rough placeholder.

name: Druze faith
summary: Esoteric monotheism; closed to converts since 1043.

summary: Song-era synthesis with Buddhist and Daoist metaphysics.

summary: Ismailis led today by the Aga Khan.

founder: Robert of Molesme; Bernard of Clairvaux
summary: Austere reformed Benedictines.

summary: Huitzilopochtli, Tlaloc, Quetzalcoatl and the sacred calendar; Templo Mayor destroyed 1521.

summary: Jurchen–Manchu clan shamanism; codified 1747.

summary: Kannada devotional reform rejecting caste and ritual.

summary: Radha-Krishna devotion.

summary: Moai, Make-make and the Birdman cult.

summary: Kurdish monotheist faith centred on Tawûsî Melek and Sheikh Adi; draws on older Iranian traditions.

name: Qadiriyya
summary: Oldest widespread Sufi order.

summary: Monastic Daoism of inner alchemy.

name: Suhrawardiyya
founder: Abu al-Najib and Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi
summary: Sufi order.

name: Waldensians
summary: Lay preaching and poverty movement; joined the Reformation in 1532.

name: Jōdo-shū

name: Beguines and Beghards
summary: Lay women (Beguines) and men (Beghards) of the Low Countries and the Rhineland who lived a religious life in the world without monastic vows, from about 1200; condemned in part at the Council of Vienne in 1311–12, they never wholly ended, and their beguinages stood in Flanders until the last traditional Beguine, Marcella Pattyn, died in 2013.

name: Chishti Order
summary: South Asian Sufi order known for music (qawwali).

name: Rinzai Zen
summary: Koan Zen.

name: Ainu religion
summary: Animist religion of the kamuy (incl. the bear ceremony).

name: Carmelite Order
summary: Hermits of Mount Carmel; reformed by Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross.

name: Chewa religion (Nyau)
summary: Gule Wamkulu masked dances (UNESCO).

name: Wixárika (Huichol) religion
summary: Peyote pilgrimage to Wirikuta and the deer-maize-peyote complex.

name: Inca religion
summary: State cult of Inti, Viracocha and the Coricancha; ended with the fall of Vilcabamba (1572).

name: Kikuyu religion
summary: Ngai of Mount Kenya.

name: Sakha religion (Aar Aiyy)
summary: Religion of the Sakha; registered as Aiyy faith in 2014.

name: Venda religion
summary: Sacred Lake Fundudzi and the python god.

name: Pawnee religion
summary: Religion of the Pawnee of the Nebraska plains, centred on Tirawahat, the power above, and on the stars and the powers of earth, sky and storm. Its best-recorded rite is the Hako, an intertribal ceremony of some twenty rituals in which a visiting party, the Fathers, carry two feathered stems and an ear of corn (Mother Corn) to their hosts, the Son and his family, and after four days and nights of songs touch, anoint and paint a child, asking Tirawa for children, long life and plenty (Fletcher, 1904: an outsider’s record).

name: Franciscan Order
summary: Mendicant order of poverty and preaching.

name: Dominican Order
summary: Order of Preachers.

name: Serbian Orthodox Church
summary: Autocephalous archbishopric since 1219.

name: Jōdo Shinshū

name: Sōtō Zen

summary: Dualist Vedanta.

summary: From the Sakya–Mongol alliance (1247) and Altan Khan's conversion (1578).

name: Alevism
summary: Anatolian tradition of Ali-devotion, cem worship and semah dance.

name: Māori religion
summary: Atua, whakapapa and tapu; Io tradition contested.

summary: Name given by the Church, from the 13th century, to groups of mystics accused of teaching that the perfected soul is one with God and above all law; condemned in 1311–12 and hunted into the 15th century. Scholars disagree about whether these were one movement or a label put on many people by their accusers.

name: Nichiren Buddhism
summary: Devotion to the Lotus Sutra's title.

name: Fraticelli (Spiritual Franciscans)
summary: Franciscans who held that Christ and the apostles owned nothing and that the order must keep the strict poverty of Francis. Pope John XXII condemned them (four Spirituals were burned at Marseille in 1318), and the Fraticelli who would not submit were hunted as heretics into the 15th century.

summary: Marathi Krishna sect.

summary: Anatolian–Balkan Sufi order.

summary: Whirling dervishes.

name: Korean Neo-Confucianism
summary: State ideology of Joseon Korea.

summary: Vietnamese Zen school.

summary: Lubaale gods (Mukasa, Kibuuka) and royal shrines.

summary: Amma, the Nommo and the 60-yearly Sigui ceremony.

summary: Sacred kingship and the Mbudye society.

summary: Kachina religion of the Hopi, Zuni and Rio Grande Pueblos.

name: Purépecha religion
summary: Curicaueri and the sacred fire.

name: Yarsanism (Ahl-e Haqq)
summary: Kurdish syncretic faith that holds the divine to have taken human form in successive manifestations; organised by Sultan Sahak.

name: Zuni (A’shiwi) religion
summary: Religion of the Zuni (A’shiwi) of western New Mexico, which Hodge’s Handbook of 1910 calls closely interwoven with their social organization: clans in seven phratral groups named for the directions, priesthoods and societies, rites in the kivas, and the masked kokko (katsina) dances. Cushing (1880s–90s) and Stevenson (1904) wrote the fullest records, an outsider’s view; the Zuni still keep their religion.

name: Hopi religion
summary: Religion of the Hopi of the three mesas of north-eastern Arizona, a yearly round of ceremonies kept by clans and societies in the kivas, with altars and dry-paintings. Hodge’s Handbook (1910) names the Soyal at the winter solstice, the Powamu bean-planting, the New Fire ceremony, the Niman at the masked spirits’ departure, the Snake–Antelope and Flute ceremonies in alternate summers and the women’s autumn ceremonies (Lagon, Oaqol, Marau): an outsider’s record.

name: Keresan Pueblo religion (Acoma, Laguna, Zia and the Rio Grande Keres)
summary: Religion of the Keresan-speaking Pueblos of New Mexico: Acoma and Laguna in the west and Zia, Santa Ana, San Felipe, Santo Domingo and Cochiti on the Rio Grande. Like the other Pueblos they hold their rites in the kivas through the year, with altars and masked dances, and the villages keep societies for curing and for the clowns; an outsider’s record (Stevenson on Zia, 1894; Hodge’s Handbook, 1910).

name: Tanoan Pueblo religion (Tewa, Tiwa and Towa)
summary: Religion of the Tanoan-speaking Pueblos: the Tewa (San Juan, Santa Clara, San Ildefonso, Nambé, Pojoaque, Tesuque, and Hano among the Hopi), the Tiwa (Taos and Picuris in the north, Sandia and Isleta in the south) and the Towa (Jemez). Its rites are kept in kivas by societies, each Tewa village has a summer half and a winter half, and the Isleta told their tales in winter (Lummis, 1894): an outsider’s record.

name: Hurufism
summary: Letter mysticism.

name: Lollardy
summary: English reform movement; precursor of the Reformation.

name: Naqshbandi Order
summary: Sufi order of silent dhikr.

name: Ni‘matullāhī order
summary: Persian Sufi order named for Shah Ni‘matullah Wali, who settled at Mahan in Kerman and died there in 1431. It spread to the Deccan in India, was revived in Iran in the late 18th century, and has branches in Iran and the West today.

name: Apache religion
summary: Usen, the Gaan mountain spirits and the Sunrise Ceremony.

name: Kubandwa (Ryangombe and Cwezi cults)
summary: Initiatory spirit cult of the Great Lakes.

name: Luo religion
summary: Nyasaye and Jok.

name: Maasai religion
summary: Enkai and the laibon prophets.

name: Mende religion (Poro and Sande)
summary: Men's Poro and women's Sande societies.

name: Midewiwin
summary: Grand Medicine Society with birch-bark scrolls.

name: Diné (Navajo) religion
summary: Hózhó (balance) restored through chantways and sandpaintings.

name: Ramanandi Sampradaya
summary: Rama devotion; largest ascetic order of North India.

name: Sant Mat
summary: North Indian devotion to the formless divine Name.

name: Kamba religion
summary: Religion of the Kamba (Akamba) of south-east Kenya: Mulungu, the high God, and the aimu, the spirits of the dead, to whom, Lindblom (1910–11) says, grain and animals are sacrificed at small huts in sacred groves, and sacrifices are made for rain in time of drought. The dates are a rough placeholder.

name: Ila religion
summary: Religion of the Ila of the Kafue plain in Zambia: Leza, the high God who sends rain and misfortune, the spirits of the dead and the diviner, as recorded by Edwin Smith and Andrew Dale in 1920. The dates are a rough placeholder.

name: Omaha religion
summary: Religion of the Omaha of the Missouri valley in Nebraska, a Siouan people whose beliefs centred on Wakonda, the great power, above the lesser powers of sun, moon, stars, earth and thunder. Fletcher and La Flesche (1911; La Flesche was himself Omaha) record the young person’s fast and prayer in a lonely place, the Sacred Pole and the Sacred Tents of War and of the White Buffalo Hide with their keepers and ritual songs, the Thunder rites, the maize ritual and the yearly buffalo hunt.

name: Hussites
summary: Bohemian reform movement.

name: Gelug
summary: School of the Dalai and Panchen Lamas.

name: Moravian Church (Unitas Fratrum)
summary: Founded 1457, renewed at Herrnhut in 1722; pioneer of Protestant missions.

name: Sthānakavāsī
summary: Image-rejecting Svetambaras.

name: Christian Kabbalah
summary: Christian reading of Kabbalah.

name: Ekasarana Dharma
summary: Assamese devotion to Krishna in satras.

name: Pushtimarg (Vallabha Sampradaya)
summary: Path of grace centred on Shrinathji.

name: Shilluk religion
summary: Divine kingship of Nyikang.

name: Mahdavia
